facts.text: The noisy miner is a large honeyeater, 24–28 centimetres long, with a wingspan of 36–45 centimetres.
facts.quote: The noisy miner is a large honeyeater, 24–28 centimetres (9.4–11.0 in) in length, with a wingspan of 36–45 centimetres (14–18 in), and weighing 70–80 grams (2.5–2.8 oz).

facts.text: It is a grey bird with a black head, bright orange-yellow beak and feet, and a distinctive patch of yellow skin behind the eye.
facts.quote: This miner is a grey bird, with a black head, orange-yellow beak and feet, a distinctive yellow patch behind the eye, and white tips on the tail feathers.

facts.text: Males, females and juveniles look similar, though young birds are a brownish-grey.
facts.quote: Males, females and juveniles are similar in appearance, though young birds are a brownish-grey.

facts.text: Living up to its name, the noisy miner is almost constantly vocal, with a large range of songs, calls, scoldings and alarms.
facts.quote: As the common name suggests, the noisy miner is a vocal species with a large range of songs, calls, scoldings and alarms, and almost constant vocalisations, particularly from young birds.

facts.text: It sings a communal 'dawn song' of clear, whistled notes in chorus in the early hours of the morning from May through January.
facts.quote: The noisy miner has a song described as the 'dawn song'—a communal song of clear, whistled notes emitted in chorus in the early hours of the morning from May through January.

facts.text: The birds live in colonies that can contain several hundred birds, foraging, bathing, roosting and breeding together.
facts.quote: they forage, bathe, roost, breed and defend territory communally, forming colonies that can contain several hundred birds

facts.text: When mobbing a potential predator, temporary flocks called coalitions can swell to up to 40 birds.
facts.quote: These flocks, called 'coalitions', usually comprise five to eight birds, although coalitions of up to 40 birds can occur when mobbing a potential predator.

facts.text: Chicks are raised communally, with males of the coterie bringing food to the nestlings and even removing their faecal sacs.
facts.quote: Looking after the young is communal, with males of the coterie bringing food to the nestlings and removing faecal sacs.

facts.text: The species has benefited from landscaping practices that create open areas dominated by eucalypts, and its populations have significantly increased in many locations.
facts.quote: studies now show that the noisy miner has benefited primarily from landscaping practices that create open areas dominated by eucalypts.
